name: itsdangerous
description: Held-out set on the real pallets/itsdangerous repository (independent history: 677 commits, 125 issues, 311 PRs, 7 releases). Questions were drafted from threads in a snapshot taken with scripts/fetch_gh_fixture.py; gold answers paraphrase those threads. No model or threshold was tuned on these items. Every item is split=test. Gold evidence is checked by scripts/check_dataset.py (refs exist in the snapshot; each key-fact group occurs in the cited evidence). Not yet verified by a second human.

items.question: Why does itsdangerous keep SHA-1 as its default digest even though SHA-1 is considered broken?
items.gold_answer: SHA-1 is only used as an intermediate step inside HMAC, where even SHA-1 and MD5 are not vulnerable; a bigger hash would only make the tokens larger without adding security.

items.question: Why were fallback signers added to itsdangerous in version 1.1?
items.gold_answer: Changing the default signing algorithm in 1.0 broke existing signatures, so 1.1 reverted to SHA-1 and added fallback signers so the algorithm can be upgraded later without invalidating existing tokens.

items.question: Why did PR #80 change the default intermediate hash from SHA-1 to SHA-512?
items.gold_answer: Mostly for aesthetics, so people would stop asking, since HMAC is still secure even with MD5; SHA-512 was picked over SHA-256 because it is more efficient on 64-bit machines.

items.question: Why was the default SHA-512 fallback signer removed?
items.gold_answer: It was only ever meant to be temporary; the switch to SHA-512 caused backwards-compatibility problems and greatly increased the size of signed values.

items.question: Why was JSON Web Signature (JWS) support removed from itsdangerous in 2.1.0?
items.gold_answer: The maintainers no longer support JWS: it was hard to maintain and often confused with JWT, and dedicated libraries such as Authlib should be used instead; it had been deprecated since 2.0.

items.question: Why did itsdangerous stop using simplejson and fall back to the standard json module?
items.gold_answer: simplejson was only needed for compatibility with old Python versions; the built-in json module is equivalent for this use, and simplejson's pure-Python fallback was a performance footgun.

items.question: Why is the SHA-1 digest in itsdangerous resolved lazily instead of at import time?
items.gold_answer: Some FIPS builds (for example certain RedHat containers) do not provide SHA-1; resolving it lazily means it fails at runtime rather than at import, giving the developer time to change the default digest before use.

items.question: Why can Signer and Serializer accept a list of secret keys?
items.gold_answer: To support key rotation: old values signed with an earlier key can still be loaded while new values are signed with the newest key in the list.

items.question: When users asked for public-key (asymmetric) signatures, what did the maintainers say to do instead of adding them?
items.gold_answer: Write a custom Signer subclass that overrides get_signature and verify_signature to use whatever signing process is wanted.

items.question: Why was Serializer made generic over str or bytes (PR #374)?
items.gold_answer: dumps had an ambiguous return type (str | bytes); making Serializer generic lets subclasses such as URLSafeSerializer be typed to always return str, so users do not need type ignores or assertions.

items.question: What did issue #137 say was wrong with the timestamps TimestampSigner writes?
items.gold_answer: It claimed TimestampSigner wrote local-time timestamps using int(time.time()) but read them back as UTC, so the timestamp and datetime conversion disagreed about the timezone.

items.question: Why did Flask users get "cannot import name 'json' from 'itsdangerous'" after upgrading to itsdangerous 2.1.0?
items.gold_answer: itsdangerous.json was deprecated in 2.0 and removed in 2.1.0; older, unsupported Flask versions still imported it. The advice was to update Flask and pin dependencies.

items.question: What crash did PR #296 fix?
items.gold_answer: An unhandled ValueError raised when a signature's timestamp was too far in the future.

items.question: Why did PR #299 catch OverflowError when parsing timestamps?
items.gold_answer: On 32-bit platforms the test for a malformed future timestamp raised OverflowError; it is now caught and raised as BadTimeSignature.

items.question: What problem did issue #410 report about URLSafeSerializer.dumps?
items.gold_answer: With a custom serializer such as msgpack it returned bytes instead of str, contradicting its type annotation of str.

items.question: What broke for users who passed salt=None after upgrading from 1.1.0 to 2.0.0?
items.gold_answer: Serializer(secret, salt=None) worked in 1.1.0 but raised an exception in 2.0.0; PR #241 allowed salt=None again.

items.question: Why was itsdangerous 1.0.0 removed from PyPI?
items.gold_answer: The maintainer yanked it because a change of the default signing algorithm made it into 1.0 and had very bad consequences, breaking existing signatures; 1.1.0 followed.

items.question: What did itsdangerous 1.1.0 change compared with 1.0?
items.gold_answer: It reverted the default to SHA-1, added a fallback mechanism for safely upgrading signing parameters later, and reverted the package name to all lowercase.

items.question: Which issue did PR #241 (allow salt=None again) fix?
items.gold_answer: Issue #237.

items.question: Which issue did PR #378 (support FIPS builds without SHA-1) fix?
items.gold_answer: Issue #375.

items.question: Which issue was PR #374 (type Serializer as generic) opened to fix?
items.gold_answer: Issue #347.

items.question: Which issue did PR #152 (remove simplejson and deprecate itsdangerous.json) close?
items.gold_answer: Issue #146.

items.question: Who opened the pull request that added support for a list of secret keys (key rotation)?
items.gold_answer: lepture.

items.question: Who reported the crash on FIPS-enabled hosts in issue #402?
items.gold_answer: cheizer.

items.question: Which digest method does Signer use by default?
items.gold_answer: SHA-1 (resolved lazily).

items.question: Which key derivation does Signer use by default?
items.gold_answer: django-concat.

items.question: What happens in TimestampSigner.unsign when a signature is older than max_age?
items.gold_answer: It raises SignatureExpired.

items.question: What does URLSafeSerializerMixin do to the payload before it is base64-encoded?
items.gold_answer: It compresses it with zlib when that makes it shorter.
